transcription.text: Hi, good afternoon. We're coming to you live from the NeoCloud Summit in San Francisco.
I'm Phoebe Liu. I'm a reporter covering AI infrastructure and semiconductors at the
Information, a tech and business publication. Joining me here is Steve Ho, head of research
at Silicon Data. Thanks for being here. Thank you very much for having me, Phoebe. Very nice to
meet you. Yeah. Would love to start by hearing a little bit more about your role. What exactly
are you researching? What kinds of things are top of mind for you in terms of kind of GPUs and
their value, which I think is, yeah. Great. So, first of all, a bit of background by myself.
As head of research at Silicon Data, I've only been this role for about four or five months.
Previously, I was head of index research at Bloomberg Indices and prior to which I was
senior research at quantum hedge fund called AQR Capital. Got my PhD in financial econometrics and
macro from the University of Michigan in 2018. So, I met Carmen Lee, the founder and CEO of
Silicon Data at Bloomberg. When she started the company in 2004, I was very curious about the
space and the whole idea is to try to bring data transparency to the otherwise fast growing,
exciting, but opaque space that is AI, right, physical AI. And we are looking at ways of
tracking and creating data to describe the various layers of the market, whether it's the compute
layer, whether it's the model layer, with terms of tokens, and also other aspects of the economics
of data centers and so on. The idea is to try to create as much data transparency as possible
and create benchmarks that can be trusted and then that becomes the basis for financial derivatives
such as futures contracts or options that could be used to then manage risk. There's a lot of
known knowledge that we want to leverage from traditional capital markets to help create more
capital efficiency in this fast growing space that is now, I think, thirsty for more financial
capital and also operating a pretty low financial capital, financial capital efficiency in various
pockets. Super interesting. We'd love to hear a little bit more about how you go about getting
your data and how you decide kind of what data goes into the indices. Yeah. So, first of all,
like in my role, I look a lot at the different types of data points that we can track that was
useful and for our GPU indices, we track all the data we can find and we primarily have two types
of data. We have quota prices and we have transaction prices. The majority of the data
points are today still quota prices and then it's a growing minority at transaction prices. We took
the deliver approach of using both types of data and the reason is because this is a market that is
still young in many ways immature. You don't get enough transactions throughout the day. If you
only use transaction data, you run the risk of being over-indexed on whether the transaction
happened to have taken place, especially if you happen to have sourced your transaction
data from a small number of providers. You're reflecting those providers pricing decisions
rather than the fall in the market. So, what we do is that to give you a quick example, if somebody
had three GPUs and they ran it out for 275 an hour, the next one I wouldn't just assume is 275. I
would take a look at what everyone else is listing. If everyone else is listing at $4 an hour, it's
supposed to be crazy to run another one to 75. Basically, you want to look at the entire market
as much as possible and recognizing also the essential features that are going to carry a
premium, whether it's location, whether it's memory, CPU, provider type, term length. The same way,
if you run it in a single measurement apartment, you will care about the location, whether you are
East Village or Soho or Harlem and you will take a simple average. You want to control these things.
The fact that a long-term contract, of course, is going to be cheaper because you are saving
that landlord, the provider, the inconvenience of having to search for a new tenant all the time.
So, that's why we use all of the above approach and to make the appropriate normalization so that
we have them maximally. Apple's comparable data points, which then consolidate into
single indices per GPU variant. How do you consolidate those into indices? Is it the
average of all the different specs and locations? How does that math work? Not asking for your
secret recipe or anything. We call it machine learning, but it is basically glorified regression
type of analysis where you essentially control for features that we deem to be important that
are generally recognized. What are the top five? Geolocation, the spec, whether it is CPU and
memory, there is also the term length. Provider type is another one. We have a number of key
features that we deem as important. Once we control for those things, we then have a pretty
stringent qualification process on the providers that we deem as being eligible. If they have
minimum number of nodes in the inventory and have minimum of 90 days of continuous reporting that
looks regular, they become eligible to be considered, at which point we have a quarterly
committee consideration to see which ones should be included. In the beginning, when the market was
relatively small, including new providers will actually lead to large adjustments in the level
of the index. Nowadays, we have almost 100 providers and the newer chips of course have fewer
because they are not as widely deployed, but generally speaking, the idea is that we have
more providers. Adding new providers will not change the level of the index very much and in
fact, that is what we see because all of large numbers kick in. Do you pay these providers for
their data? Is that how that works? It depends on the provider. The smallest providers, they
voluntarily give us data in exchange for their market intelligence where we provide them with
anonymized market intelligence at the market level for pricing and various reasons. The
modestly bigger ones, we do half in-kind, half commercial and then for the very big ones,
of course, there will be commercial agreements struck on whether or not it is full or incomplete
or visibility. That's why we said it is a growing process. Some providers initially are, I think,
hesitant about the idea of providing data, but then I think generally people are now getting
on board with the idea that transparency is a good thing and it is going to make the market
more trustworthy and the bigger market fundamentally is much better for everybody.
You guys were the first GPU index, but now there are also others. What makes you different?
I think different people have different approaches to data, a source of data, how they want to hand
the data. Some people take the deliver approach of only including transactions. I think that you
can also tell when you just plot the two indices side by side. On the normal terminal, for example,
you see some of the variants being listed and there is a reason why. Some are more volatile
than others and that comes down to design choice. More broadly, I think there are
methodological differences as well that goes beyond data source. We take the pretty deliberate
approach thinking about this as a financial benchmark that could be trusted and I guess
that's our differentiation. That makes sense. I saw a chart that I think you posted on X
recently about some token prices going down quite a bit over this last quarter and that
kind of affecting anthropics ARR. Can you break that down for us? That index caught quite a bit
of attention. It's our token index. It's actually kind of a misnomer. People misunderstand it. It's
either a price index or a volume index. It's actually neither. It is an expenditure-weighted
price index that tells you the average price of the models being used to normalize your million
tokens. You can almost think of it as like imagine this is not tokens. This is like a car company.
They sell a luxury car and it's a normal ordinary car. The ordinary sedan suddenly gets a lot of
adoption because cars are now being widely used. That's going to pull down the average of the price
of the car sold. But meanwhile, you're going to see a lot more cars on the street. The same thing
here. If you have cheap flash models that are being widely deployed and that's satiating the
everyday tasks, that's going to comprise the vast majority of the tokens used. We will normally
normalize, but it's going to also pull down the price of the model and also probably the margin
of the model to the extent that these frontier labs really charge the most and sort of get the
best margin from their most powerful models and face competition as you come down in model
capabilities. That's probably not great for their valuation. This is all fundamentally
juxtaposing valuation with fundamentals. Anybody would love to have the level of growth even as
today that Enthropy enjoys, but we are already being valued at somewhere between one to two
trillion dollars. I think then you start giving people a bit of pause on whether or not the
exponential growth on the ARR, so to speak, the revenue growth can be sustained if there is
increasing competition and usage makes shifting away from frontier reasoning towards everyday
agentic use. Super interesting, and last just curious macro question for me. If prices for
GPUs per hour end up going back down, how do you think that will kind of affect the AI economy to
be super proud about it? So it depends on the reason, right? So you know, generally speaking,
even though GPU rental per hour per cheap variant is going up, all of the rental rates are going up,
but even A100's rental rate is going up since the start of the year now is holding about steady,
and then B200, B300 have gone up significantly over the last few months. But if you think about
from a total super point of view how much you're actually getting per GPU hour, you're getting way
more intelligence and getting way more number of tokens on the more expensive chips. So in a sense,
market is quite intelligence rational about the fact that you pay more because you get more output
per hour. And do you measure GPU kind of usefulness over time? Because you have an index to do that,
right? We have a silicon mark, which is a fiscal benchmark. It's not an index. Is it ongoing though?
It is ongoing. We continuously monitor GPU performance and health throughout the globe,
you know, in a random sample fashion in order to, you know, because we are anticipating eventually
moving towards a world of physically delivered futures. And more on that, stay tuned. But in the
meantime, but your question regarding whether the compute price is going down, I think that is a
different question. If all of the compute front end rental rates start going down, you can have a
scenario where, you know, maybe demand for AI isn't, you know, quite catching up with supply. I mean,
that's the trillion dollar, literally the trillion dollar question, right? You know, everyone is
currently anticipating that there's going to be continuously exponential growth in demand,
whereas supply is growing linearly with all sorts of headwinds coming from not just physical
constraints, power, lack of space, but also political pushback. Do you feel like today there
are chips that are sitting there not able to be plugged in and turned on? I mean, we don't
track that per se, but we have seen news reports of due to a lack of power and the various physical
constraints and you're unable to deploy all of the chips, you know, that may be available. So today,
people say that the shortage is not in the chip anymore, but in power and other forms of, you know,
like cooling system and so on. And Elon is running around the world looking for turbines.
Yes. Well, we'll end it there. Thank you so, so much for your insight. Really appreciate it.
Thank you very much for your time.
